occurrences.source_problem:
For a surface $S$ given by $y=2x{z}^{3}$ for $(x,z)\in D,$ the flux of the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{D}(\,{z}^{3}+Q-\,x{z}^{2})\,\text{d}A.
$$

From left to right, what are the missing parts of the formula?

*Hint: The orientation of $S$ should be chosen such that the unit normal vector has a positive  $j$-component.*
occurrences.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Since our surface $S$ is of the form $y=2x{z}^{3},$ it can be parameterized as

$$
r(x,z)=⟨x,\,2x{z}^{3},z⟩.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′} & =⟨1,\,2{z}^{3},\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{z}^{′} & =⟨0,\,6x{z}^{2},\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{z}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 2{z}^{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 6x{z}^{2} & 1\end{aligned}|=⟨2{z}^{3},\,-1,\,6x{z}^{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

However, notice that the $j$-component is negative. Therefore, we select the normal vector that points in the *opposite* direction:

$$
{r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{x}^{′}=-{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{z}^{′}=⟨-2{z}^{3},\,1,\,-6x{z}^{2}⟩
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(x,z))\cdot ({r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{x}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨P,\,Q,R\,⟩\cdot ⟨-2{z}^{3},\,1,\,-6x{z}^{2}⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-2P\,{z}^{3}+Q-6R\,x{z}^{2}\,)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{}-Q\frac{∂g}{}+R)\,\text{d}A.
$$

From left to right, what are the missing parts of the formula?
prepared_question.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Since our surface $S$ is of the form $z=g(x,y),$ it can be parameterized as

$$
r(x,y)=⟨x,\,y,\,g(x,y)⟩.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′} & =⟨1,\,0,\,\frac{∂g}{∂x}⟩ \\ {r}_{y}^{′} & =⟨0,\,1,\,\frac{∂g}{∂y}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{y}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & \frac{∂g}{∂x} \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{∂g}{∂y}\end{aligned}|=⟨-\frac{∂g}{∂x},\,-\frac{∂g}{∂y},\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(x,y))\cdot ({r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{y}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩\cdot ⟨-\frac{∂g}{∂x},\,-\frac{∂g}{∂y},\,1⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the surface integral

$$
{∬}_{S}⟨\frac{1}{z},\,\frac{xy}{z},\,z⟩\cdot \text{d}S
$$

where the surface $S$ is defined by $z={e}^{x-y}$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le x.$
occurrences.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ given by $z=g(x,y)$ for $(x,y)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}{e}^{x-y}={e}^{x-y} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}{e}^{x-y}=-{e}^{x-y}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x,y,g(x,y)) & =⟨\frac{1}{z},\,\frac{xy}{z},\,z⟩{|}_{z={e}^{x-y}} \\  & =⟨{e}^{-(x-y)},\,xy{e}^{-(x-y)},\,{e}^{x-y}⟩ \\  & =⟨{{{e}^{y-x}}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{xy{e}^{y-x}}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{{e}^{x-y}}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can evaluate our surface integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨\frac{1}{z},\,\frac{xy}{z},\,z⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-{e}^{y-x}\cdot {e}^{x-y}-(xy{e}^{y-x})\cdot (-{e}^{x-y})+{e}^{x-y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-1+xy+{e}^{x-y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x}(-1+xy+{e}^{x-y})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[-y+\frac{x{y}^{2}}{2}-{e}^{x-y}]}_{y=0}^{y=x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-x+\frac{{x}^{3}}{2}-1+{e}^{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{x}^{4}}{8}-x+{e}^{x}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{8}-1+e)-1 \\  & =-\frac{19}{8}+e\end{aligned}
$$

occurrences.source_problem:
Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $T,$ where $T$ is defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}u+2w \\ v-u \\ uw\end{aligned}].
$$
occurrences.worked_solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=u+2w,\,y(u,v,w)=v-u,\,z(u,v,w)=uw.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =2 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =w & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =u\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ w & 0 & u\end{aligned}| \\  & =1|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & u\end{aligned}|+2|\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ w & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =1(u-0)+2(0-w) \\  & =u-2w.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ u-2w & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $u-2w=0$ defines the plane $u=2w.$

choices.value: The critical points lie on the plane $u=2w.$
The critical points lie on the plane $u+v-2w=0.$
The critical points lie on the $vw-$ plane.
The critical points lie on the elliptic cylinder ${u}^{2}+2{w}^{2}=1.$
The critical points lie on the parabolic cylinder $v={u}^{2}.$

before_fields.submitted_value: The critical points lie on the elliptic cylinder ${u}^{2}+2{w}^{2}=1.$

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{u}^{2}-{w}^{2} \\ w{e}^{u} \\ u-v\end{aligned}].
$$
occurrences.worked_solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)={u}^{2}-{w}^{2},\,y(u,v,w)=w{e}^{u},\,z(u,v,w)=u-v.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =-2w \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =w{e}^{u} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & ={e}^{u} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}2u & 0 & -2w \\ w{e}^{u} & 0 & {e}^{u} \\ 1 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =2u|\begin{aligned}0 & {e}^{u} \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}|-2w|\begin{aligned}w{e}^{u} & 0 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =2u(0+{e}^{u})-2w(-w{e}^{u}-0) \\  & =2u{e}^{u}+2{w}^{2}{e}^{u} \\  & =2{e}^{u}({w}^{2}+u).\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ 2{e}^{u}({w}^{2}+u) & =0 \\ {w}^{2}+u & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation ${w}^{2}+u=0$ defines the parabolic cylinder $u=-{w}^{2}.$

The solid enclosed by the quarter-sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=9$ for $x\ge 0$ and $y\le 0,$ shown above, can be described in spherical polar coordinates as
occurrences.worked_solution:
We write the position of a point (vector) in spherical polar coordinates as $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ),$ where 

- $\rho \ge 0$ is the distance from the point to the origin,

- $\theta \in [0,2\pi )$ is the angle between the point and the positive $x$-axis, and

- $ϕ\in [0,\pi ]$ is the angle the corresponding vector makes with the positive $z$-axis.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093183/assets/d338181a6631c513330ef2dd3899cfb9b01cb6f4c4ff7d9cd65038b381e7fec4.png)

  

Notice that inside our region, the spherical polar coordinates vary withing the following domains:

- $\rho \in [0,3]$

- $\theta \in [\frac{3\pi }{2},2\pi ]$

- $ϕ\in [0,\pi ]$

Therefore, we have

$$
{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 3,\,\frac{3\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 2\pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi }.
$$

Consider the vector field $F=⟨y,\,0,\,2x⟩$ and the closed surface $S$ that represents the boundary of the solid shown above. Let $D$ be the projection of the solid onto the $xy$-plane. The flux of $F$ across $S$ can be expressed in terms of a double integral as 

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∬}_{D}\,\,\text{d}A.
$$

Which of the following could be the missing expression?
occurrences.worked_solution:
Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So,

- the upper surface ${S}_{1}:z=g(x,y)=0$ is oriented upward, and

- the lower surface ${S}_{2}:z=h(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-2$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

- Consider the upper plane ${S}_{1}.$ 

Since the positive orientation is upward, the unit normal vector to the plane is $n=⟨0,0,1⟩.$ As a result, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨y,0,2x⟩\cdot ⟨0,0,1⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2x\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

- Consider the lower cone ${S}_{2}.$

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=h(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-2)=\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}} \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-2)=\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=y,\,Q=0,\,R=2x.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is downward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & =-{∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂h}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂h}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}(-y\cdot \frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}-0\cdot \frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}+2x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{xy}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}-2x)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux across the entire surface is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}2x\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}(\frac{xy}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}-2x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{xy}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the vector field $F=⟨1,\,z,\,0⟩$ and the closed surface $S$ that encloses the finite region between the parabolic cylinders $z=4{x}^{2}$ and $z=16-4{y}^{2}.$ Let $D$ be the projection of $S$ onto the $xy$-plane. The flux of $F$ across $S$ can be expressed in terms of a double integral as 

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∬}_{D}\,\,\text{d}A.
$$

Which of the following could be the missing expression?
occurrences.worked_solution:
Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So,

- the upper surface ${S}_{1}:z=g(x,y)=16-4{y}^{2}$ is oriented upward, and

- the lower surface ${S}_{2}:z=h(x,y)=4{x}^{2}$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

- Consider the upper cylinder ${S}_{1}.$

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(16-4{y}^{2})=0 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(16-4{y}^{2})=-8y\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=1,\,Q=z=16-4{y}^{2},\,R=0.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-1\cdot 0-(16-4{y}^{2})\cdot (-8y)+0)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(128y-32{y}^{3})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

- Consider the lower cylinder ${S}_{2}.$ 

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=h(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4{x}^{2})=8x \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4{x}^{2})=0\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=1,\,Q=z=4{x}^{2},\,R=0.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is downward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & =-{∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂h}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂h}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}(-1\cdot 8x-4{x}^{2}\cdot 0+0)\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}-8x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}8x\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux across the entire surface is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}(128y-32{y}^{3})\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}8x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}128y-32{y}^{3}+8x\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

occurrences.source_problem:
Consider the finite region $R$ in the $xyz$-space, given by

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x+3y\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le z-3y\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le z\le 2}.
$$

Given the change of variables

$$
u=x+3y,\,v=z-3y,\,w=z,
$$

which of the following could be the missing part of the expression below?

$$
{∭}_{R}{cos}^{2}⁡(x+z)\operatorname{cos}⁡(z-3y)\,dV={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2}\,dw\,dv\,du
$$
occurrences.worked_solution:
Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space.

To find the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\text{ }dV={∭}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))\,|\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=x+3y,\,v=z-3y,\,w=z
$$

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y,z) \\ v(x,y,z) \\ w(x,y,z)\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the required integral, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & ={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le u\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le v\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le w\le 2}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =1|\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =1(-3-0) \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{3}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}{cos}^{2}⁡(x+z)\operatorname{cos}⁡(z-3y)\,dV & ={∭}_{Δ}{cos}^{2}⁡(u+v)\operatorname{cos}⁡v\cdot |\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w \\  & ={∭}_{Δ}{cos}^{2}⁡(u+v)\operatorname{cos}⁡v\cdot |-\frac{1}{3}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2}\,\frac{1}{3}{cos}^{2}⁡(u+v)\operatorname{cos}⁡v\,\,dw\,dv\,du\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14094456/assets/1422e6534c001214335dcddb8888f7e2e9344e440379c47da38514e9a3ef0bd8.png)

Consider the vector field $F=⟨z,\,0,\,2⟩$ and the closed surface $S$ that represents the boundary of the solid shown above. Let $D$ be the projection of $S$ onto the $xy$-plane. The flux of $F$ across $S$ can be expressed in terms of a double integral as 

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∬}_{D}\,\,\text{d}A.
$$

Which of the following could be the missing expression?
occurrences.worked_solution:
Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So, 

- the upper surface ${S}_{1}:z=g(x,y)=1-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ is oriented upward, and

- the lower surface ${S}_{2}:z=h(x,y)=0$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

- Consider the upper cone ${S}_{1}.$

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(1-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}})=-\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(1-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}})=-\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=z=1-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},\,Q=0,\,R=2.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-(1-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}})\cdot (-\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}})-0\cdot (-\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}})+2\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}-x+2\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

- Consider the lower plane ${S}_{2}.$ 

Since the positive orientation is downward, the unit normal vector to the plane is $n=⟨0,0,-1⟩.$ As a result, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨z,0,2⟩\cdot ⟨0,0,-1⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-2\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux of $F$ across the entire surface is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}-x+2\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}-2\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}-x\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14073713/assets/e2ab6906100a96a123b4b1520613f1e38fe2c7e77af390a8efe0596a2861727d.png)

Consider the linear transformation $T$ with matrix representation $T,$ given by

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

What would be the image of the triangle shown above under the action of $T?$
occurrences.worked_solution:
Recall that for any linear transformation $T$ with associated $2\times 2$ matrix $T,$ we have one of the following three possibilities:

- If $T$ is non-singular, i.e., $det(T)\ne 0,$ then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with $n$ vertices is a polygon with $n$ vertices.

- If $T$ is singular, i.e., $det(T)=0,$ we have two additional subcases:

- If $T$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

- If $T$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is the point $(0,0),$ the origin of the coordinate system.

Since $T$ is the zero matrix, the image of our object under the action of $T$ is the origin.

choices.value: A point, different from the origin
The origin $O$ of the coordinate system

Let $C$ be the intersection of the surface $z=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}$ and the boundary of the infinite vertical column enclosed by the planes $x=\pm 1,$ and $y=\pm 1.$ Given that the curve $C$ is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above and $\text{curl}\,F=⟨x,\,y,\,-2z⟩,$ the circulation of $F$ along $C$ can be written as 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr=
$$
occurrences.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the surface $z=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}$ and the boundary of our infinite vertical column. One such surface is our surface $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1})=\frac{-2x}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1})=\frac{-2y}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨x,\,y,\,-2z⟩{|}_{z=1/({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)} \\  & =⟨{{x}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{y}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-x\cdot \frac{-2x}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}-y\cdot \frac{-2y}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-\frac{2}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071512/assets/b215ec1e3330f96e7e606e085721b2dd1f50d113f0151e36ec98e6d0a6f54e73.png)

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}-\frac{2}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{1}\,-\frac{2}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

occurrences.source_problem:
The curvature of the plane curve $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+t\,j$ is given by 

$$
κ(t)=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{},\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

 
What is the missing part of the expression?
occurrences.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ(t)$ of a plane curve $r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{|{x}^{′}(t){y}^{″}(t)-{y}^{′}(t){x}^{″}(t)|}{([{x}^{′}(t)]^{2}+[{y}^{′}(t)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

Along our curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(t)=t.
$$

First, we calculate the derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\, & {y}^{′}(t) & =1 \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\, & {y}^{″}(t) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the curvature, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{|(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot 0-(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot 1|}{{((\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+{1}^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{|\operatorname{cos}⁡t|}{{({sin}^{2}⁡t+1)}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{\sqrt{{({sin}^{2}⁡t+1)}^{3}}}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we removed the absolute value because cosine is positive for $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].$

k(t)=\frac{{x}^{′}(t){y}^{″}(t)-{y}^{′}(t){x}^{″}(t)}{([{x}^{′}(t)]^{2}+[{y}^{′}(t)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

Along our curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,y(t)=-{t}^{2}.
$$

First, we calculate the derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\, & {y}^{′}(t) & =-2t \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\, & {y}^{″}(t) & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the signed curvature, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}k(t) & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (-2)-(-2t)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}{{((\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(-2t)^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2t\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{{({cos}^{2}⁡t+4{t}^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{2(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}{\sqrt{({cos}^{2}⁡t+4{t}^{2})^{3}}}\end{aligned}
$$

occurrences.source_problem:
Which of the following is a stream function for the vector field
$F(x,y)=2{x}^{2}y\,i-2x{y}^{2}\,j?$
occurrences.worked_solution:
A vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ with a simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2}$ has a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ if and only if

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.
$$

Note that $F(x,y)=2{x}^{2}y\,i-2x{y}^{2}\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D={R}^{2},$ where $P(x,y)=2{x}^{2}y$ and $Q(x,y)=-2x{y}^{2}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=4xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-4xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $F$ has a stream function, since

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=4xy+(-4xy)=0.
$$

Next, we find a stream function. A function $ψ(x,y)$ is a stream function of the vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ if 

$$
P=\frac{∂ψ}{∂y},\,Q=-\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\frac{∂ψ}{∂y}=2{x}^{2}y,\,\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}=2x{y}^{2}.
$$

Integrating these equations, we obtain the following:

$$
ψ(x,y)={x}^{2}{y}^{2}+f(x),\,ψ(x,y)={x}^{2}{y}^{2}+g(y)
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are arbitrary functions. Finally, setting $f=g=0,$ we have

$$
ψ(x,y)={x}^{2}{y}^{2}=(xy)^{2}.
$$

occurrences.source_problem:
Let $S$ be the boundary of the rectangular prism enclosed by the planes $x=-1,$ $x=0,$ $y=1,$ $y=2,$ $z=0,$ $z=1.$ Given that the surface $S$ is positively (outward) oriented and $F=xy\,i+2y\,j+{x}^{2}zk,$ the flux of $F$ across $S$ can be written as 

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\,\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.
$$

What is the missing part of the expression?
occurrences.worked_solution:
Let $R$ be a simple solid region bounded by a closed surface $S$ with positive (outward) orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $R,$ then the divergence theorem states that

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∭}_{R}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}V.
$$

Computing the divergence of $F,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y)+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}z) \\  & =y+2+{x}^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}+y+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $R$ be the solid region enclosed by $S.$ Then, using the divergence theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS & ={∭}_{R}({x}^{2}+y+2)\,\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\,{x}^{2}+y+2\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

The graph of the function $z=f(x,y)$ is shown above. Which of the points shown are local minimum points?
occurrences.worked_solution:
A function $f(x,y)$ has a local minimum point at $(a,b)$ if $f(x,y)\ge f(a,b)$ for all points $(x,y)$ in a neighborhood of $(a,b).$ 

In other words, we can take a neighborhood of $(x,y)$-values such that the point $(x,y,f(x,y))$ is the lowest point on the graph in the neighborhood.

Such regions exist for the points $A$ and $D.$ Hence $A$ and $D$ are local minimum points.

**Note**: For the point $D({x}_{D},{y}_{D},{z}_{D}),$ there are points $(x,y)$ in the surrounding regions such that $f({x}_{D},{y}_{D})=f(x,y).$ However, since the definition of local extrema is non-strict, $f(x,y)\ge f(a,b)$, the point $D$ does satisfy the conditions for a local minimum.

**Note**: For the point $D({x}_{D},{y}_{D},{z}_{D}),$ there are points $(x,y)$ in the surrounding regions such that $f({x}_{D},{y}_{D})=f(x,y).$ However, since the definition of local extrema is non-strict, $f(x,y)\ge f(a,b)$, the point $D$ does satisfy the conditions for a local minimum.

Then, the corresponding Lagrange multipliers $\lambda $ and $\mu $ satisfy the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}⟨2x,\,2yz,\,{y}^{2}⟩=\lambda ⟨\,,\,0,\,2z⟩+\mu ⟨0,\,,\,1⟩ \\ {x}^{2}+{z}^{2}=1 \\ {y}^{2}+z=9\end{aligned}

From left to right, what are the missing expressions?

$$
f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}z
$$

 

subject to the constraints 

$$
g(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{z}^{2}=1,\,h(x,y,z)={y}^{2}+z=9.
$$

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\ g(x,y,z)=1 \\ h(x,y,z)=9\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x},{f}_{y},{f}_{z}⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x},{g}_{y},{g}_{z}⟩+\mu ⟨{h}_{x},{h}_{y},{h}_{z}⟩ \\ ⟨2x,\,2yz,\,{y}^{2}⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,\,0,\,2z⟩+\mu ⟨0,\,2y,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

occurrences.source_problem:
For the transformation $f:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{3},$ defined as

$$
f(x)=[\begin{aligned}xy \\ {x}^{2}-y \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}],
$$

the total derivative ${f}^{′}$ is given by 

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}y &  \\  & -1 \\  & x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)\end{aligned}].
$$

From top to bottom, what are the missing entries?
occurrences.worked_solution:
Suppose a transformation $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{m}$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{f}_{1}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ {f}_{2}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ ⋮ \\ {f}_{m}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})\end{aligned}],
$$

 

where ${f}_{1},{f}_{2},…,{f}_{m}$ are scalar functions with $n$ variables. If $f$ is differentiable at $x,$ then the total derivative of $f$ at $x,$ denoted ${f}^{′}(x),$ is given by the $m\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have the following:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂y}\end{aligned}]
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy)=y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy)=x, \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-y)=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-y)=-1, \\ \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy))=y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy),\, & \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy))=x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}y & x \\ 2x & -1 \\ y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy) & x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)\end{aligned}].
$$

Thus, the missing entries are $x,\,$ $2x,\,$ and $y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy).$

occurrences.source_problem:
The quadratic Taylor approximation of the function $f(x)$ about $x=a\in {R}^{3}$ is given by

$$
f(x)≈-\frac{4}{3}+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}](x-a).
$$

Given that the eigenvalues of ${f}^{″}(a)$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=1,{\lambda }_{2}=2,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=3,$ what type of point is $a?$
occurrences.worked_solution:
The point $a\in {R}^{n}$ is a critical point of the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}.$ In such cases, we can classify $a$ as follows:

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is positive definite, then $a$ is a local minimum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is negative definite, then $a$ is a local maximum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, then $a$ is a saddle point

The quadratic Taylor expansion of a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ about $x=a\in {R}^{n}$ given by

$$
f(x)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a).
$$

Since the quadratic Taylor expansion of $f$ has no $(x-a)$ term, we can conclude that ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}.$ Hence, $a$ is a critical point of $f.$

Finally, notice that all the eigenvalues of ${f}^{″}(a)$ are positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & =1>0 \\ {\lambda }_{2} & =2>0 \\ {\lambda }_{3} & =3>0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the matrix is positive definite. Therefore, $a$ is a local minimum of $f.$

The graph $z=f(x,y)$ is shown above. What are the global maximum points of the function?
occurrences.worked_solution:
First, we recall the following definitions:

- The global maximum of a function is the largest value it attains on its domain. There can only be (at most) one global maximum.

- A global maximum point is a point $(x,y,z)$ where a function reaches a global maximum. There can be zero, one, or many global maximum points.

For our function, the maximum value reached by the function is $f(x,y)=3.$ Therefore, the global maximum is $3.$ The function reaches this value when $(x,y)=(-2,1),$ so the global maximum point is $(-2,1,3).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070363/assets/215b322e06280dd01e5858df9a17cd56673b5cdec69521decca205e03771ac21.png)

The graph $z=f(x,y)$ is shown above. What are the global maximum points of the function?
prepared_question.worked_solution:
First, we recall the following definitions:

- The global maximum of a function is the largest value it attains on its domain. There can only be (at most) one global maximum.

- A global maximum point is a point $(x,y,z)$ where a function reaches a global maximum. There can be zero, one, or many global maximum points.

For our function, the maximum value reached by the function is $f(x,y)=3.$ Therefore, the global maximum is $3.$ The function reaches this value when $(x,y)=(-2,1),$ so the global maximum point is $(-2,1,3).$

The graph of the function $z=f(x,y)$ is shown above. Which of the points shown are local maximum points?
occurrences.worked_solution:
A function $f(x,y)$ has a local maximum point at $(a,b)$ if $f(x,y)\le f(a,b)$ for all points $(x,y)$ in a neighborhood of $(a,b).$ 

In other words, we can take a neighborhood of $(x,y)$-values such that the point $(x,y,f(x,y))$ is the highest point on the graph in the neighborhood.

Such neighborhoods exist for the points $C$ and $D.$ Hence $C$ and $D$ are local maxima.

occurrences.source_problem: What is the radius of the sphere $(x-2)^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}-4z=12?$
occurrences.worked_solution:
Remember that the equation of a sphere centered at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ with radius $r>0$ is given by

$$
(x-{x}_{0})^{2}+(y-{y}_{0})^{2}+(z-{z}_{0})^{2}={r}^{2}.
$$

By completing the square for the variable $y$, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-2)^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}-4z & =12 \\ (x-2)^{2}+{y}^{2}+({z}^{2}-4z+4) & =12+4 \\ (x-2)^{2}+{y}^{2}+(z-2)^{2} & =16\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can write our equation as

$$
(x-2)^{2}+{y}^{2}+(z-2)^{2}={4}^{2},
$$

which gives us a radius of $4.$

occurrences.source_problem: Given the ellipsoid $\frac{(x+2)^{2}}{8}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}+\frac{(z-2)^{2}}{16}=1$, find its intercepts with the $y$-axis.
occurrences.worked_solution:
To find the $y$-intercepts, we plug $x=0$ and $z=0$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(0+2)^{2}}{8}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}+\frac{(0-2)^{2}}{16} & =1 \\ \frac{4}{8}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}+\frac{4}{16} & =1 \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{4} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {y}^{2} & =1 \\ y & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we get the solutions $y=-1$ and $y=1.$

Therefore, the intercepts with the $y$-axis are $(0,-1,0)$ and $(0,1,0).$

occurrences.source_problem: Given the hyperboloid of two sheets ${x}^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}-\frac{(z+1)^{2}}{4}=-1,$ find its $z$-intercepts.
occurrences.worked_solution:
To find the $z$-intercepts, we plug $x=0$ and $y=0$ into the equation: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{0}^{2}+\frac{{0}^{2}}{2}-\frac{(z+1)^{2}}{4} & =-1 \\ -\frac{(z+1)^{2}}{4} & =-1 \\ (z+1)^{2} & =4 \\ z+1 & =\pm 2 \\ z & =-1\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we get the solutions $z=-3$ and $z=1.$

Therefore, the intercepts with the $z$-axis are $(0,0,-3)$ and $(0,0,1).$

occurrences.source_problem: Given the sphere $(x-3)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}+(z-2)^{2}=9,$ what is the domain of $z=z(x,y)?$
occurrences.worked_solution:
From the equation of the sphere, we make $z$ the subject as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-3)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}+(z-2)^{2} & =9 \\ (z-2)^{2} & =9-((x-3)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}) \\ z-2 & =\pm \sqrt{9-((x-3)^{2}+(y-1)^{2})} \\ z & =2\pm \sqrt{9-((x-3)^{2}+(y-1)^{2})}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the square root is defined only for non-negative arguments, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}9-((x-3)^{2}+(y-1)^{2})\ge 0 \\ (x-3)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}\le 9\end{aligned}
$$

This inequality describes the interior and boundary of the circle 

$$
(x-3)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=9
$$

which is a circle of radius $3$ centered at $(3,1)$ in the $xy$-plane.

occurrences.source_problem: What is the trace in the $yz$-plane of the parabolic cylinder $(x+3)^{2}=6y?$
occurrences.worked_solution:
To find the trace in the $yz$-plane, we substitute $x=0$ into the equation of the cylinder, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}(0+3)^{2} & =6y \\ 9 & =6y \\ y & =\frac{9}{6} \\ y & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of a line in the $yz$-plane.

occurrences.source_problem: What is the trace in the $xz$-plane of the elliptic cylinder $\frac{(x-4)^{2}}{8}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{2}=1?$
occurrences.worked_solution:
To find the trace in the $xz$-plane, we substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the cylinder, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x-4)^{2}}{8}+\frac{(0-1)^{2}}{2} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-4)^{2}}{8}+\frac{1}{2} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-4)^{2}}{8} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ (x-4)^{2} & =4 \\ x-4 & =\pm 2 \\ x & =4\pm 2 \\ x & =2,6\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of two lines $x=2$ and $x=6$ in the $xz$-plane.

occurrences.source_problem:
Identify the following surface: 

$$
\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{9}+\frac{(y+2)^{2}}{7}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{4}=1
$$
occurrences.worked_solution:
Recall that the equation of an ellipsoid centered at $O$ is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{{c}^{2}}=1,
$$

and an ellipsoid centered at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ is given by

$$
\frac{(x-{x}_{0})^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{(y-{y}_{0})^{2}}{{b}^{2}}+\frac{(z-{z}_{0})^{2}}{{c}^{2}}=1,
$$

Thus, our equation is an ellipsoid with the following parameters:

$$
({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})=(1,-2,0),\,a=3,\,b=\sqrt{7},\,c=2.
$$

occurrences.source_problem: The projection of the intersection between the parabolic cylinder $3(x+2)^{2}=6(y+3)$ and the plane $z=4$ onto the $xy$-plane is a parabola. What is the vertex of the parabola?
occurrences.worked_solution:
To find the intersection of the cylinder and the plane $z=4,$ we substitute $z=4$ into the equation of the cylinder. However, since the equation has no (explicit) $z$ term, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3(x+2)^{2} & =6(y+3) \\ (x+2)^{2} & =2(y+3) \\ (x+2)^{2} & =4\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot (y+3).\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of a parabola in the $xy$-plane with the vertex at $(-2,-3).$

occurrences.source_problem: What is the domain in the $xy$-plane of the hyperbolic cylinder $\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{4}=1?$
occurrences.worked_solution:
The full expression describing all points on our hyperbolic cylinder is

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{4}=1,\,z=k
$$

where $k\in R$ can vary arbitrarily. 

The domain of any cylinder in the $xy$-plane is its base curve. Hence, in this case, the domain is

$$
{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}:\text{ }\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{4}=1}.
$$

This is a hyperbola centered at $(0,-1).$

occurrences.source_problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}+4t,3{t}^{2}+9t⟩,$ find the point at which the tangent to the curve is parallel to the vector $⟨1,3⟩.$
occurrences.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}+4t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2}+9t)⟩ \\  & =⟨3t+4,6t+9⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})=c⟨1,3⟩.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =c⟨1,3⟩ \\ ⟨3t+4,6t+9⟩ & =c⟨1,3⟩ \\ ⟨3t+4,6t+9⟩ & =⟨c,3c⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components gives:

$$
{\begin{aligned}3t+4=c \\ 6t+9=3c\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we obtain that $c=3t+4.$ Substituting $c=3t+4$ into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}6t+9 & =3(3t+4) \\ 6t+9 & =9t+12 \\ 3t & =-3 \\ t & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $⟨1,3⟩$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the point corresponding to $t=-1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-1) & =⟨\frac{3}{2}(-1)^{2}+4(-1),3(-1)^{2}+9(-1)⟩=⟨-\frac{5}{2},-6⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨1,3⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $(-\frac{5}{2},-6).$

occurrences.source_problem: Find the global extrema of the function $f(x,y)=1-{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ on the closed region $D={(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 16}.$
occurrences.worked_solution:
Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$

To find the extreme values, we follow three steps.

**Step 1.** Find the critical points of $f$ inside the region. 

To determine the critical points, we solve ${f}^{′}=0.$ Computing the derivative gives

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}-2x,\,2y\end{aligned}].
$$

The derivative exists at each point inside $D,$ and it equals zero when

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}-2x=0 \\ 2y=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}x=0 \\ y=0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us a single point $(0,0)\in D,$ which we include in the list of candidates for the extrema.

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of $D$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the boundary points that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize the bounding circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16.$ This gives

$$
r=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,t\in [0,2\pi ).
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =1-(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =1-16{cos}^{2}⁡t+16{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =1-16\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\in (0,2\pi ),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ (1-16\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)^{′} & =0 \\ 32\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The final equation gives four solutions, namely

$$
t=\frac{\pi }{2},\,\pi ,\,\frac{3\pi }{2}\in (0,2\pi ).
$$

We also have to check the endpoint of the interval $t=0.$ Therefore, the only values of $t$ that can give rise to extreme values are 

$$
t=0,\,\frac{\pi }{2},\,\pi ,\,\frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

Evaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ on the boundary, we obtain four candidate points:

$$
(4,0),\,(0,4),\,(-4,0),\,(0,-4)
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values. 

Evaluating $f(x,y)$ at each of the points mentioned above, we get the following: 

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,0)$ | $(4,0)$ | $(0,4)$ | $(-4,0)$ | $(0,-4)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $1$ | $-15$ | $17$ | $-15$ | $17$ |

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $-15$ at the points $(4,0)$ and $(-4,0),$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $17$ at the points $(0,4)$ and $(0,-4).$

occurrences.source_problem: Calculate the $x$-coordinates of the points where the hyperbola ${x}^{2}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}=1$ intersects the line $y=8x.$
occurrences.worked_solution:
To find the points where the hyperbola intersects the line $y=8x,$ we first replace $y$ with $8x$ in the equation of the hyperbola and solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{16} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}-\frac{(8x)^{2}}{16} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}-\frac{64{x}^{2}}{16} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}-4{x}^{2} & =1 \\ -3{x}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2} & =-\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

We cannot take the square root of a negative number. Therefore, the equation has no real solutions. So, the hyperbola does not intersect the line $y=8x.$

choices.value: There are no points of intersection

occurrences.source_problem:
$\,$ $3\,|\,18$ or $11$ is not prime.

What is the negation of the compound statement above?
occurrences.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for disjunctions states that the negation of a disjunction of two statements is equivalent to the conjunction of the negations of the individual statements. It can be stated symbolically as follows:

$$
¬(A∨B)=¬A∧¬B.
$$

So, the negation of our statement is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(3\,|\,18\text{ or }11\text{ is not prime}) & ≡¬((3\,|\,18)∨(11\text{ is not prime})) \\  & ≡¬(3\,|\,18)∧¬(11\text{ is not prime}) \\  & ≡(3\,\text{⧸}|\,18)∧(11\text{ is prime}) \\  & ≡3\,\text{⧸}|\,18\text{ and }11\text{ is prime}.\end{aligned}
$$

occurrences.source_problem:
$\,$ $x=3$

The predicate $P(x)$ is given above. Which of following represents $¬P(x)?$
occurrences.worked_solution:
In plain English, our predicate $P(x)$ means the following:

$\,$ $x$ equals $3.$

The symbol "$¬$" represents negation. To negate our plain English expression, we place the words "It is not true that" in front of it. This gives the following:

$\,$ It is not true that $x$ equals $3.$

In other words, $x$ is *not equal to* $3.$ Therefore, $¬P(x)$ means the following:

$\,$ $x\ne 3$

occurrences.source_problem: Find the center of the elliptic cone $4(x-3)^{2}+5(y+2)^{2}=20(z-1)^{2}.$
occurrences.worked_solution:
The general equation of an elliptic cone with center at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ is

$$
\frac{(x-{x}_{0})^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{(y-{y}_{0})^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=\frac{(z-{z}_{0})^{2}}{{c}^{2}}.
$$

To find the center, we rewrite our equation in standard form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}4(x-3)^{2}+5(y+2)^{2} & =20(z-1)^{2} \\ \frac{(x-3)^{2}}{1/4}+\frac{(y+2)^{2}}{1/5} & =\frac{(z-1)^{2}}{1/20} \\ \frac{(x-3)^{2}}{1/4}+\frac{(y-(-2))^{2}}{1/5} & =\frac{(z-1)^{2}}{1/20}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of an elliptic cone that has its center at $(3,-2,1).$

occurrences.source_problem: Identify the sentence that is equivalent to the following: "$x$ is rational, and $x$ is less than $2$ and it is rational."
occurrences.worked_solution:
Using the commutative law, we can replace the phrase "$x$ is less than $2$ and it is rational" with the phrase "$x$ is rational and it is less than $2.$" The sentence now reads

"$x$ is rational, and $x$ is rational and it is less than $2.$"

Then, using the associative law, we can move the comma:

"$x$ is rational and $x$ is rational, and it is less than $2.$"

Now, we can simplify the phrase "$x$ is rational and $x$ is rational" to just "$x$ is rational." The sentence now reads

"$x$ is rational, and it is less than $2.$"

Finally, we can write the sentence more concisely:

"$x$ is rational and less than $2.$"

choices.value: $x$ is rational but not less than $2$
$x$ is neither rational nor less than $2$

First, we need to factor the polynomial. For this polynomial, we can factor by grouping:

$$
\begin{aligned}p(x) & ={x}^{3}-5{x}^{2}-25x+125 \\  & ={x}^{2}(x-5)-25(x-5) \\  & =({x}^{2}-25)(x-5) \\  & =(x+5)(x-5)(x-5) \\  & =(x-5{)}^{2}(x+5)\end{aligned}
$$

To find the roots and their multiplicities, we look at the factors:

- The factor $(x-5)$ has an exponent of $2$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=5$ has multiplicity $2.$

- The factor $(x+5)$ has an exponent of $1$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=-5$ has multiplicity $1.$

In conclusion, only the root $x=5$ has multiplicity $2.$

occurrences.source_problem: Use the first three terms of the binomial expansion of $(1+x)^{7}$ in ascending powers of $x$ to approximate $(0.99)^{7}.$ Give your answer to four decimal places.
occurrences.worked_solution:
Recall that when $n$ is a positive integer, 

$$
(1+x)^{n}=1+nx+\frac{1}{2!}n(n-1){x}^{2}+⋯+{x}^{n}.
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{(1+x)}^{7} & =1+7x+\frac{1}{2}\cdot 7\cdot 6\cdot {x}^{2}+⋯+{x}^{7} \\  & =1+7x+21{x}^{2}+⋯+{x}^{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, for small $x,$ we have

$$
{(1+x)}^{7}≈1+7x+21{x}^{2}.
$$

Finally, we substitute $x=-0.01$ into the above approximation of $(1+x)^{7}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}(0.99)^{7} & =(1+(-0.01))^{7} \\  & ≈1+7(-0.01)+21(-0.01)^{2} \\  & =1-7(0.01)+21(0.000\,1) \\  & =1-0.07+0.002\,1 \\  & =0.932\,1,\end{aligned}
$$

to four decimal places.

occurrences.source_problem: Which set is equivalent to $S={0,{1},{0},1,0,{0}}?$
occurrences.worked_solution:
Two sets are equivalent if they contain the same elements. It doesn't matter if the elements are listed differently or if one set has duplicates and the other does not.

To determine which of the given sets is equivalent to $S,$ we start by listing the elements of $S,$ ignoring any duplicates:

$$
0,\,{1},\,{0},\,1
$$

Therefore, the only set equivalent to $S$ is ${0,1,{0},{1}}$ since it contains the same elements as $S.$

The other sets are not equivalent to $S:$

- ${0,1,{1}}$ is missing the element ${0}$ (note that ${0}\ne 0$).

- ${{0},0,1}$ is missing the element ${1}$ (note that ${1}\ne 1$).

- ${0,1,{0,1},{0},{1}}$ has the element ${0,1}$ that is not in $S.$

- ${0,1,{1},2,{0}}$ has the element $2$ that is not in $S.$

occurrences.source_problem:
Which of the following sets are infinite?

- $A={n\in Z\,:\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{2})=1}$
- $B={q\in Q\,:\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{q\pi }{2})=1}$
- $C={x\in R\,:\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x\pi }{2})=1}$
occurrences.worked_solution:
The cardinality of a finite set is the number of elements contained within it. A set is infinite if it has infinitely many elements.

We start by finding the solutions to the equation $\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x\pi }{2})=1$ for $x\in R:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x\pi }{2} & =2m\pi  \\ x & =4m,\,m\in Z\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our sets:

- The set $A$ is infinite. Listing the elements of $B$ for different values of $m,$ we have

$$
A={…,-4,0,4,8,…}.
$$

- The set $B$ is infinite. Since $A$ is infinite, and $A⊆B,$ it follows that $B$ is infinite.

- The set $C$ is infinite. Since $B$ is infinite, and $B⊆C,$ it follows that $C$ is infinite.

Therefore, the correct answer is "$A,$ $B,$ and $C.$"

occurrences.source_problem:
$\,$ $|{1,x}|\ne 0$ and $x$ is rational

What is the negation of the compound statement above?
occurrences.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law posits that the negation of a conjunction of two statements is equivalent to the disjunction of the negated individual statements. It can be stated symbolically as follows.

$$
¬(A∧B)=¬A∨¬B
$$

So, the negation of our statement is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(|{1,x}|\ne 0\text{ and }x\text{ is rational}) & ≡¬((|{1,x}|\ne 0)∧(x\text{ is rational})) \\  & ≡¬(|{1,x}|\ne 0)∨¬(x\text{ is rational}) \\  & ≡(|{1,x}|=0)∨(x\text{ is not rational}) \\  & ≡|{1,x}|=0\text{ or }x\text{ is not rational}.\end{aligned}
$$

$\,$ $2$ is not prime or $2\notin Q.$

What is the negation of the compound statement above?

De Morgan's law for disjunctions states that the negation of a disjunction of two statements is equivalent to the conjunction of the negations of the individual statements. It can be stated symbolically as follows:

$$
¬(A∨B)=¬A∧¬B
$$

So, the negation of our statement is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(2\text{ is not prime}\text{ or }2\notin Q) & ≡¬((2\text{ is not prime})∨(2\notin Q)) \\  & ≡¬(2\text{ is not prime})∧¬(2\notin Q) \\  & ≡(2\text{ is prime})∧(2\in Q) \\  & ≡2\text{ is prime}\text{ and }2\in Q.\end{aligned}
$$

occurrences.source_problem:
$\,$ If you exercise regularly, then you'll improve your health.

Which statement is logically equivalent to the conditional statement above?
occurrences.worked_solution:
Let's denote by $A$ and $B$ the following statements:

- $A:$ You exercise regularly.

- $B:$ You will improve your health.

Then, our initial statement can be written as $A⇒B,$ which is logically equivalent to 

$$
¬A∨B.
$$

The negation of $A$ can be written as

- $¬A:$ You do not exercise regularly.

Therefore, the given statement is logically equivalent to the following:

$\,$ You do not exercise regularly, or you will improve your health.

We can write this in more everyday language as follows:

$\,$ Either you do not exercise regularly, or you'll improve your health.

**Note**: 

Using the word "Either" helps clarify that the sentence structure presents two alternatives and is particularly useful when employing the disjunctive form $(¬P∨Q)$ in conversational or formal English. So, the phrase effectively conveys that one of the two stated conditions will hold true.

occurrences.source_problem:
Describe the set $S={…,3,6,12,24,48,...}$ using a constructive definition.

*Hint: Take ${a}_{1}=6$ in the sequence that generates the elements of $S.$*

$$
\frac{2}{3}\cdot {3}^{n}
$$
occurrences.worked_solution:
Notice that the elements of our set

$$
…,\,3,\,6,\,12,\,24,\,48,\,…
$$

form a two-way infinite geometric sequence with a common ratio $r=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =2 \\  & =\frac{6}{3} \\  & =\frac{12}{6} \\  & =\frac{24}{12} \\  & =⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, setting  ${a}_{1}=6,$ the $n$th term ${a}_{n}$ of our sequence for $n\in Z$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =6\cdot {2}^{n-1} \\  & =6\cdot {2}^{n}\cdot {2}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{6}{2}\cdot {2}^{n} \\  & =3\cdot {2}^{n}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can define our set using a constructive definition as follows:

$$
S={3\cdot {2}^{n}\,:\,n\in Z}
$$

occurrences.source_problem:
$\,$ If $x\in N,$ then  $x$ is positive.

Which of the following is logically equivalent to the conditional predicate above?
occurrences.worked_solution:
Let's denote by $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ the following predicates:

- $P(x):$ $x\in N.$

- $Q(x):$ $x$ is positive.

Then, our initial sentence can be written as $P(x)⇒Q(x),$ which is logically equivalent to 

$$
¬P(x)∨Q(x).
$$

The negation of $P(x)$ can be written as

- $¬P(x):$ $x\notin N.$

Therefore, the given sentence is logically equivalent to the following:

$\,$ $x\notin N,$ or $x$ is positive.

occurrences.source_problem:
Negate the following statement:

$\,$ For all $t\in Q,$ $t<1.$
occurrences.worked_solution:
If we denote

$$
P(t):t<1,
$$

our statement can be written as

$$
∀t\in Q,\,P(t).
$$

Negating this, we obtain

$$
¬(∀t\in Q,\,P(t))≡∃t\in Q,\,¬P(t).
$$

Finally, $∃t\in Q,\,¬P(t)$ reads as follows:

$\,$ **There exists** $t\in Q$ such that $t\ge 1.$

$$

which reads

$\,$ Some prime numbers are divisible by $5.$

occurrences.source_problem:
Describe the set $S={...,3,6,9,12,15,...}$ using a constructive definition.

*Hint: Take ${a}_{1}=3$ in the sequence that generates the elements of $S.$*

$$
n+2
$$
occurrences.worked_solution:
Notice that the elements of our set

$$
…,\,3,\,6,\,9,\,12,\,15,\,…
$$

form a two-way infinite arithmetic sequence with common difference $d=3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =3 \\  & =6-3 \\  & =9-6 \\  & =12-9 \\  & =⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, setting  ${a}_{1}=3,$ the $n$th term ${a}_{n}$ of our sequence for $n\in Z$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)\cdot d \\  & =3+(n-1)\cdot 3 \\  & =3+3n-3 \\  & =3n.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can define our set using a constructive definition as follows:

$$
S={3n\,:\,n\in Z}
$$

$$

Therefore, we can define our set using a constructive definition as follows:

$$
S={(-2)^{n}\,:\,n\in Z}
$$

occurrences.source_problem:
Negate the following statement:

$\,$ There exists $y\in R$ such that $\frac{y}{2}$ is not real.
occurrences.worked_solution:
If we denote

$$
P(y):\frac{y}{2}\text{ is real},
$$

our statement can be written as

$$
∃y\in R,\,¬P(y).
$$

Negating this, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(∃y\in R,\,¬P(y)) & ≡∀y\in R,\,¬¬P(y) \\  & ≡∀y\in R,\,P(y).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $∀y\in R,\,P(y)$ reads as follows:

$\,$ **For all** $y\in R,$ $\frac{y}{2}$ is real.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14046771/assets/33e48fa5bdbb034bcf489e038ccf80fc5f67baabeccacc1b7abd741183ebf05d.png)

Consider the square region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane, given by

$$
Δ={(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,0\le v\le 1},
$$

and the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:(u,v)\to (x(u,v),y(u,v)),
$$

where 

$$
x=v(2-u),\,y=u{v}^{3}.
$$

The image of the side ${S}_{3}$ under the action of $T$ is given by

$$
x=x(t),\,y=t,\,1\ge t\ge 0.
$$

Find the function $x(t).$
occurrences.worked_solution:
To map the entire region $Δ$ onto the $xy$-plane, we consider the transformation of each side. However, in this case, we consider only the side ${S}_{3}.$

For the side ${S}_{3},$ we have $1\ge u\ge 0$ and $v=1.$ Substituting $v=1$ into our transformation equations, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y) & =T(u,v) \\  & =(v(2-u),\,u{v}^{3}) \\  & =(1(2-u),\,u(1)^{3}) \\  & =(2-u,u).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the image of ${S}_{3}$ can be parametrized by

$$
x=2-u,\,y=u,\,1\ge u\ge 0.
$$

 

Writing this in the usual notation, we have

$$
x(t)=2-t,\,y(t)=t,\,1\ge t\ge 0.
$$

Consider the square region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane, given by

$$
Δ={(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,0\le v\le 1},
$$

and the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:(u,v)\to (x(u,v),y(u,v)),
$$

where 

$$
x=\frac{v-1}{u+1},\,y=(u+v-1)^{2}+1.
$$

Which of the following is the image of the side ${S}_{4}$ under the action of $T?$
occurrences.worked_solution:
To map the entire region $Δ$ onto the $xy$-plane, we consider the transformation of each side. However, in this case, we consider only the side ${S}_{4}.$

For the side ${S}_{4},$ we have $u=0$ and $1\ge v\ge 0.$ Substituting $u=0$ into our transformation equations, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y) & =T(u,v) \\  & =(\frac{v-1}{u+1},\,(u+v-1)^{2}+1) \\  & =(\frac{v-1}{0+1},\,(0+v-1)^{2}+1) \\  & =(v-1,\,(v-1)^{2}+1).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the image of ${S}_{4}$ can be parametrized by

$$
x=v-1,\,y=(v-1)^{2}+1,\,1\ge v\ge 0.
$$

 

Writing this in the usual notation, we have

$$
x=t-1,\,y=(t-1)^{2}+1,\,1\ge t\ge 0.
$$

These are parametric equations of a parabolic arc. Notice that if we eliminate $t$ from the equations, we get

$$
y={x}^{2}+1
$$

which is an upward-opening parabola whose vertex is at $(0,1).$

Moreover, the endpoints of ${S}_{4}$ are mapped to the $xy$-plane as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & T:(0,1)\to (\frac{1-1}{0+1},(0+1-1)^{2}+1)=(0,1) \\  & T:(0,0)\to (\frac{0-1}{0+1},(0+0-1)^{2}+1)=(-1,2)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the image of ${S}_{4}$ is an arc of a upward-opening parabola, traversed from $(0,1)$ to $(-1,2).$

occurrences.source_problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}=2xy,\,y(1)=1
$$

We wish to approximate the solution using the modified Euler method. What entry should be placed in the cell indicated in the table below, if the step size is $Δx=1?$

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $1$ |  |  |  |  |  |
| $2$ | $\,?\,$ |  |  |  |  |  |
occurrences.worked_solution:
For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,{y}_{0}=y({x}_{0}),
$$

the Modified Euler Method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Predictor} & : & Δ{y}_{p} & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx, \\ \text{Corrector} & : & Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{p}^{′})\cdot Δx,\end{aligned}
$$

where ${y}_{p}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{p})$ is the initially predicted slope at the predicted new point $({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{p})=(x+Δx,y+Δ{y}_{p}).$

First, we compute the value of ${y}^{′}$ according to the given rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =2xy \\  & =2\cdot 1\cdot 1 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So, we add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $1$ | $2$ |  |  |  |  |

Next, we compute $Δ{y}_{p}$ using the predictor equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ{y}_{p} & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx \\  & =2\cdot 1 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $1$ | $2$ | $2$ |  |  |  |

The coordinates of the initially predicted new point given by the predictor equation are

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=1+1=2, \\ {y}_{\text{pred}} & =y+Δ{y}_{\text{pred}}=1+2=3.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's add the second value to the table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $1$ | $2$ | $2$ | $3$ |  |  |

So, the predicted slope at this point is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & =2\cdot {x}_{\text{new}}\cdot {y}_{p} \\  & =2\cdot 2\cdot 3 \\  & =12.\end{aligned}
$$

We can add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $1$ | $2$ | $2$ | $3$ | $12$ |  |

Finally, we compute $Δy$ using the corrector equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{p}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2+12)\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 14 \\  & =7\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $1$ | $2$ | $2$ | $3$ | $12$ | $7$ |

The value of $x$ in the next row is ${x}_{\text{new}}=2.$ To get the value of $y$ in the next row, we add $Δy$ to $y:$

$$
{y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy=1+7=8.
$$

Adding these results to our table gives the following:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $1$ | $2$ | $2$ | $3$ | $12$ | $7$ |
| $2$ | $8$ |  |  |  |  |  |

Therefore, we conclude that $y(2)≈8.$

occurrences.source_problem:
Find the general solution to the system of differential equations 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)={x}_{1}(t)+3{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)={x}_{1}(t)-{x}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

*Hint: The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$*
occurrences.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].$

- We are given that the eigenvalues are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-2\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=2.
$$

- Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-2,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{2}I=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].

occurrences.source_problem:
Consider the system of linear differential equations given by

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}]x(t).
$$

Given that the solution to the system can be written as

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}a \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}a \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-t}+[\begin{aligned}b \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $a+b?$
occurrences.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}].$

Since $A$ is lower-triangular, the repeated eigenvalue is $\lambda =-1$ (of multiplicity two).
For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution of the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ [\begin{aligned}-1-(-1) & 0 \\ 3 & -1-(-1)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}0{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2}=0 \\ 3{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{1}=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

The variable ${w}_{2}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{2}=0,$ we get 

$$
w=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-t}+[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Finally, we see that $a=0,b=\frac{1}{3},$ and $a+b=\frac{1}{3}.$

occurrences.source_problem: Find the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{3t}-{e}^{-t}$ for $s>3.$
occurrences.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)}
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{3t}-{e}^{-t}} & =L{{e}^{3t}}+L{-{e}^{-t}} \\  & =L{{e}^{3t}}-L{{e}^{-t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we recall the following result:

$$
L{{e}^{kt}}=\frac{1}{s-k},\,s>k
$$

 
Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{3t}} & =\frac{1}{s-3},\,s>3 \\ L{{e}^{-t}} & =\frac{1}{s+1},\,s>-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{{e}^{3t}}-L{{e}^{-t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{s-3}-\frac{1}{s+1} \\  & =\frac{(s+1)-(s-3)}{(s-3)(s+1)} \\  & =\frac{s+1-s+3}{(s-3)(s+1)} \\  & =\frac{4}{(s-3)(s+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $L{{e}^{3t}}$ is defined for $s\in (3,\infty )$ and $L{{e}^{-t}}$ is defined for $s\in (-1,\infty ),$ we have that $L{f(t)}$ is defined for

$$
(3,\infty )\cap (-1,\infty )=(3,\infty ),
$$

that is, $s>3.$

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{3t}-{e}^{-t}} & =L{{e}^{3t}}+L{-{e}^{-t}} \\  & =L{{e}^{3t}}-L{{e}^{-t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we recall the following result:

$$
L{{e}^{kt}}=\frac{1}{s-k},\,s>k
$$

 
Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{3t}} & =\frac{1}{s-3},\,s>3 \\ L{{e}^{-t}} & =\frac{1}{s+1},\,s>-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{{e}^{3t}}-L{{e}^{-t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{s-3}-\frac{1}{s+1} \\  & =\frac{(s+1)-(s-3)}{(s-3)(s+1)} \\  & =\frac{s+1-s+3}{(s-3)(s+1)} \\  & =\frac{4}{(s-3)(s+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $L{{e}^{3t}}$ is defined for $s\in (3,\infty )$ and $L{{e}^{-t}}$ is defined for $s\in (-1,\infty ),$ we have that $L{f(t)}$ is defined for

$$
(3,\infty )\cap (-1,\infty )=(3,\infty ),
$$

that is, $s>3.$

Consider a function $b(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $L{b(t)}=B(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Suppose we wish to find $L{{e}^{t}b(t)}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write 

$$
{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{-t}b(t)
$$
occurrences.worked_solution:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{t}b(t)} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{t}\,b(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-1)t}\,b(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $B(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,b(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-1)t}\,b(t)\,\text{d}t=B(s-1),
$$

where 

$$
s-1>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}+1.
$$

occurrences.source_problem: Consider a function $f(t)$ for which the Laplace transform is $L{f(t)}=F(s).$ How can we obtain the graph of $L{{e}^{-9t}f(t)}$ from the graph of $F(s)?$
occurrences.worked_solution:
The first shifting theorem states that if
$L{f(t)}=F(s),$
then
$L{{e}^{at}f(t)}=F(s-a).$

This implies that multiplying a function $f(t)$ by ${e}^{at}$ shifts the corresponding Laplace transform horizontally along the $s$-axis.

- If $a>0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the right.

- If $a<0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the left.

In our case, to get the graph of $L{{e}^{-9t}f(t)},$ we must shift the graph of $F(s)$ by $9$ units to the left.

Consider the following inhomogeneous system of linear differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]x(t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]
$$

The complementary solution to this system is given by

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

occurrences.worked_solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

The forcing term

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]
$$

of the inhomogeneous system of ODEs is sinusoidal. Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal, i.e.

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{aligned}]+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)[\begin{aligned}{b}_{1} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

where ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{b}_{1},{b}_{2}$ are constants that are to be determined.

occurrences.source_problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}=2x+2y-1,\,y(0)=1
$$

We wish to approximate the solution using the $2$-step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton Method. What entry should be placed in the cell indicated in the table below, where the first step has already been computed using the Runge-Kutta method, if the step size is $Δx=1?$

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $5$ |
| $1$ | $6$ |  |  |  |  |  |
| $2$ | $\,?\,$ |  |  |  |  |  |

*Hint: The corrector equation of the two-step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton method is defined as*

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{12}(5{y}_{p}^{′}+8{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx
$$

*where ${y}_{p}$ denotes the predictor at the current step, and ${y}_{-1}^{′}$ is the estimated slope at the previous point.*
occurrences.worked_solution:
For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c,
$$

the $2$-step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton (ABM2) method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Predictor} & : & Δ{y}_{p} & =\frac{1}{2}(3{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx, \\ \text{Corrector} & : & Δy & =\frac{1}{12}(5{y}_{p}^{′}+8{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx,\end{aligned}
$$

where

- ${y}^{′}=f(x,y)$ is the estimated slope at the current point $(x,y),$

- ${y}_{-1}^{′}=f({x}_{-1},{y}_{-1})$ is the estimated slope at the previous point $({x}_{-1},{y}_{-1}),$ and

- ${y}_{p}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{p})$ is the estimated slope at the predicted new point $({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{p})=(x+Δx,y+Δ{y}_{p}).$

We're told that the first step is calculated using the Runge-Kutta Method, resulting in 

$$
y(1)≈6.
$$

Now, we'll continue from this point, using the ABM $2$-step method.

First, we compute the value of ${y}^{′}$ according to the given rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =2x+2y-1 \\  & =2\cdot 1+2\cdot 6-1 \\  & =13.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $5$ |
| $1$ | $6$ | $13$ |  |  |  |  |

From the first row of the table, we see that the slope at the previous point $({x}_{-1},{y}_{-1})=(0,1)$ is ${y}_{-1}^{′}=1.$

Next, we compute $Δ{y}_{p}$ using the predictor equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ{y}_{p} & =\frac{1}{2}(3{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(3\cdot 13-1)\cdot 1 \\  & =19.\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $5$ |
| $1$ | $6$ | $13$ | $19$ |  |  |  |

So, the coordinates of the predicted new point are

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=1+1=2, \\ {y}_{p} & =y+Δ{y}_{p}=6+19=25.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's add the second value to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $5$ |
| $1$ | $6$ | $13$ | $19$ | $25$ |  |  |

Hence, the slope at this predicted point is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & =2{x}_{\text{new}}+2{y}_{p}-1 \\  & =2\cdot 2+2\cdot 25-1 \\  & =53.\end{aligned}
$$

We can add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $5$ |
| $1$ | $6$ | $13$ | $19$ | $25$ | $53$ |  |

Finally, we compute $Δy$ using the corrector equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{12}(5{y}_{p}^{′}+8{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{12}(5\cdot 53+8\cdot 13-1)\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{12}\cdot 368 \\  & =\frac{92}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $5$ |
| $1$ | $6$ | $13$ | $19$ | $25$ | $53$ | $\frac{92}{3}$ |

The value of $x$ in the next row is ${x}_{\text{new}}=2.$ To get the value of $y$ in the next row, we add $Δy$ to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\  & =6+\frac{92}{3} \\  & =\frac{110}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Adding these results to our table gives the following:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $5$ |
| $1$ | $6$ | $13$ | $19$ | $25$ | $53$ | $\frac{92}{3}$ |
| $2$ | $\frac{110}{3}$ |  |  |  |  |  |

Therefore, we conclude that $y(2)≈\frac{110}{3}.$

We wish to approximate the solution using the $2$-step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton Method. What entry should be placed in the cell indicated in the table below, where the first step has already been computed using the Runge-Kutta method, if the step size is $Δx=1?$

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $5$ |
| $1$ | $6$ |  |  |  |  |  |
| $2$ | $\,?\,$ |  |  |  |  |  |

*Hint: The corrector equation of the two-step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton method is defined as*

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{12}(5{y}_{p}^{′}+8{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx
$$

*where ${y}_{p}$ denotes the predictor at the current step, and ${y}_{-1}^{′}$ is the estimated slope at the previous point.*
prepared_question.worked_solution:
For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c,
$$

the $2$-step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton (ABM2) method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Predictor} & : & Δ{y}_{p} & =\frac{1}{2}(3{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx, \\ \text{Corrector} & : & Δy & =\frac{1}{12}(5{y}_{p}^{′}+8{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx,\end{aligned}
$$

where

- ${y}^{′}=f(x,y)$ is the estimated slope at the current point $(x,y),$

- ${y}_{-1}^{′}=f({x}_{-1},{y}_{-1})$ is the estimated slope at the previous point $({x}_{-1},{y}_{-1}),$ and

- ${y}_{p}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{p})$ is the estimated slope at the predicted new point $({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{p})=(x+Δx,y+Δ{y}_{p}).$

We're told that the first step is calculated using the Runge-Kutta Method, resulting in 

$$
y(1)≈6.
$$

Now, we'll continue from this point, using the ABM $2$-step method.

First, we compute the value of ${y}^{′}$ according to the given rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =2x+2y-1 \\  & =2\cdot 1+2\cdot 6-1 \\  & =13.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $5$ |
| $1$ | $6$ | $13$ |  |  |  |  |

From the first row of the table, we see that the slope at the previous point $({x}_{-1},{y}_{-1})=(0,1)$ is ${y}_{-1}^{′}=1.$

Next, we compute $Δ{y}_{p}$ using the predictor equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ{y}_{p} & =\frac{1}{2}(3{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(3\cdot 13-1)\cdot 1 \\  & =19.\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $5$ |
| $1$ | $6$ | $13$ | $19$ |  |  |  |

So, the coordinates of the predicted new point are

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=1+1=2, \\ {y}_{p} & =y+Δ{y}_{p}=6+19=25.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's add the second value to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $5$ |
| $1$ | $6$ | $13$ | $19$ | $25$ |  |  |

Hence, the slope at this predicted point is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & =2{x}_{\text{new}}+2{y}_{p}-1 \\  & =2\cdot 2+2\cdot 25-1 \\  & =53.\end{aligned}
$$

We can add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $5$ |
| $1$ | $6$ | $13$ | $19$ | $25$ | $53$ |  |

Finally, we compute $Δy$ using the corrector equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{12}(5{y}_{p}^{′}+8{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{12}(5\cdot 53+8\cdot 13-1)\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{12}\cdot 368 \\  & =\frac{92}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $5$ |
| $1$ | $6$ | $13$ | $19$ | $25$ | $53$ | $\frac{92}{3}$ |

The value of $x$ in the next row is ${x}_{\text{new}}=2.$ To get the value of $y$ in the next row, we add $Δy$ to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\  & =6+\frac{92}{3} \\  & =\frac{110}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Adding these results to our table gives the following:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $5$ |
| $1$ | $6$ | $13$ | $19$ | $25$ | $53$ | $\frac{92}{3}$ |
| $2$ | $\frac{110}{3}$ |  |  |  |  |  |

Therefore, we conclude that $y(2)≈\frac{110}{3}.$
